newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Investors queue for slice of NZ fast food chain.
newsitem.headline: Investors queue for slice of NZ fast food chain.

text.p: Investors are queueing for a slice of the action in a rare initial public offering (IPO) involving the spin-off of Pepsico Inc's New Zealand restaurant chains.
The new company, Restaurant Brands New Zealand Ltd, is due to list on June 4 in what will be the biggest float in the country since Tranz Rail Holdings Ltd debuted last June.
Unlike Tranz Rail, which was a partial float, Restaurant Brands will be offered in its entirety. The company will be the only fast food franchise operation on the New Zealand exchange.
The float of 85 million shares at between NZ$1.80-2.20 each will value the company at NZ$187 million (US$130 million) if the tender values them at the top of the range.
It should also take the company into the New Zealand Stock Exchange's top 40 stocks by market capitalisation, and thus the key market index.
Graeme Cavanagh, a partner at lead manager FR Partners, said the issue had been well-supported and there was a chance it would be oversubscribed.
"It's in the early stages, but it is getting a lot of retail and institutional support," he said.
New York-based Pepsico will be selling a free-standing company that controls 122 KFC and Pizza Hut stores across New Zealand.

The move to go public is a separate but parallel move to Pepsico's wider plan to divest the KFC, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut brands in their entirety. The firm says it believes franchisees get better results from running restaurants in the long run.
KFC and Pizza Hut are two of the three largest fast food chains in New Zealand, the other being McDonalds.
Total sales last year were NZ$221 million, 80 percent coming from the chicken-based KFC chain and 20 percent from Pizza Huts.
KFC has enjoyed strong growth since entering the market here in 1971, long before arch burger rival, McDonalds, but Pizza Hut has not performed as well, industry analysts say.
Internationally, Pepsico had been developing new formats designed for Pizza Hut, which were likely to be emulated here under the franchise deal, Restaurant Brands chairman Bill Falconer told Reuters.

Pepsico's move to demerge its New Zealand assets has a parallel. In 1993 troubled Wang Laboratories spun Wang New Zealand off, only for the stock to end up three years later back in U.S. hands with the takeover by U.S. Office Products.
Falconer said it was possible, but unlikely, that Restaurant Brands might meet the same fate. For the take out company to itself be "taken out" represented only a minor risk, he added.
Falconer said it was inevitable that there would be foreign investors among the future shareholder base, particularly from U.S. institutions familiar with the brands.
The new firm's chairman, with a background in New Zealand's oil and gas industry, has made a move into retail-oriented company boardrooms in recent years.
However, he said he saw parallels between oil and fast food, with both requiring continual evolution.
Analysts say the restaurant trade is notoriously fickle -- a new product can boom one year and slump the next.
"That's particularly true of the fast food business. You've got to constantly rotate your product," Falconer told Reuters.
Restaurant Brands' has meanwhile made a commitment to Pepsico, as its franchiser, to expand the number of stores to 37 over the next 10 years.
This arrangement may prove onerous, some market observers have said, particularly if there is a squeeze on market share.
But Falconer said market share was not necessarily the sole arbiter of sales and profit growth. He said it was likely that Restaurant Brands would exceed the contract requirement.
The issue's promoters said the level of fast food penetration in New Zealand is much lower than in comparable economies, leaving plenty of room to grow.
